variants.title: Run the edge release
variants.context: An edge release moves from a frozen device contract to an exported and signed artifact, to measured evidence on real devices, to a cohort-by-cohort rollout, and finally to offline operation where inference and rollback stay bounded without connectivity.
variants.prompt: A model that scores well in a notebook is proposed for a phone fleet. Put the deployment steps in order.

items.text: Export and inspect: convert the model, validate signatures and operators, sign the bundle, and bind it to compatible runtime versions.
Profile the real path: measure load, preprocessing, warm inference, postprocessing, peak memory, energy, heat, and task quality on representative devices.
Freeze the contract: name supported cohorts, quality floors, latency deadlines, resource ceilings, fallback behavior, and release owners.
Operate offline: keep inference and rollback bounded without connectivity and queue versioned telemetry for reconciliation.
Release by cohort: canary the exact bundle, enforce independent gates, retain the known-good version, and stop promotion on failure.

variants.hint: What has to be written down before any measurement can be called a pass or a fail?
variants.explanation: The contract defines what the evidence must prove, so freezing it first is what turns profiling numbers into release decisions.

variants.title: Run the edge release
variants.context: An edge release moves from a frozen device contract to an exported and signed artifact, to measured evidence on real devices, to a cohort-by-cohort rollout, and finally to offline operation where inference and rollback stay bounded without connectivity.
variants.prompt: A driver update lands on one hardware cohort and the support matrix changes. Put the required work in order.

items.text: Confirm the offline rollback path still restores a compatible known-good version on those devices.
Update the frozen support matrix so the new driver and runtime versions are named cohort fields.
Re-profile load, warm latency, peak memory, and task quality on devices carrying the new driver.
Canary the unchanged bundle to that cohort alone with its own gates.
Re-bind the signed artifact to the runtime versions it is now certified against.

variants.hint: A cohort field changed, so which evidence is now stale?
variants.explanation: Any change to model, runtime, app, OS, driver, or hardware invalidates the evidence for that cohort and forces a re-run.

variants.title: Run the edge release
variants.context: An edge release moves from a frozen device contract to an exported and signed artifact, to measured evidence on real devices, to a cohort-by-cohort rollout, and finally to offline operation where inference and rollback stay bounded without connectivity.
variants.prompt: A microcontroller product must keep working through multi-day network outages. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Bound telemetry retention locally and reconcile the queued, versioned records when the network returns.
Sign the bundle and bind it to the exact runtime build that will be flashed with it.
Measure cold load, warm inference, peak working set, and sustained thermal behavior on the real board.
Freeze offline behavior and rollback expectations as named product limits in the contract.
Stage the release to a canary batch while the previous known-good image stays resident on each device.

variants.hint: A rollback is only real if it works with no network at all.
variants.explanation: Offline operation is part of the contract, so the known-good artifact stays on the device and telemetry is bounded rather than unbounded.

variants.title: Promote through cohorts
variants.context: A fleet rollout is a sequence of independent release decisions, not a percentage slider. Each stage preserves its own evidence, expands only when every gate passes for the current cohort, stops automatically when telemetry or a critical signal fails, and restores an already-tested compatible artifact.
variants.prompt: An immutable bundle is ready for a mixed fleet. Put the rollout stages in order.

items.text: Roll back affected devices to an already-tested compatible artifact.
Confirm artifact integrity, model load, backend placement, memory, warm latency, thermal behavior, energy, and task quality.
Diagnose by model, app, runtime, OS, driver, hardware, region, and input cohort before rebuilding.
Expand only when every required gate passes for the current cohort.
Start with hardware canaries that span the support matrix.
Stop automatically when telemetry disappears or a critical signal crosses its declared limit.

variants.hint: Expansion is a decision that has to be earned by the current cohort's evidence.
variants.explanation: Each stage is an independent release decision, so promotion waits on that cohort's gates and failure halts the sequence rather than continuing on an average.

variants.title: Promote through cohorts
variants.context: A fleet rollout is a sequence of independent release decisions, not a percentage slider. Each stage preserves its own evidence, expands only when every gate passes for the current cohort, stops automatically when telemetry or a critical signal fails, and restores an already-tested compatible artifact.
variants.prompt: A canary cohort stops reporting telemetry while its last known metrics looked healthy. Put the controller's actions in order.

items.text: Rebuild only after the cohort that went dark is reproduced and explained.
Halt promotion so no further devices become eligible for the candidate.
Restore the affected devices to the retained known-good artifact.
Treat the missing telemetry as a failed gate rather than as a silent pass.
Segment the silence by app, runtime, OS, driver, hardware, and region to find the shared cohort field.

variants.hint: Absent evidence is not the same as good evidence.
variants.explanation: A rollout stops automatically when telemetry disappears, because a fleet-wide average cannot see a cohort that has stopped reporting at all.

variants.title: Promote through cohorts
variants.context: A fleet rollout is a sequence of independent release decisions, not a percentage slider. Each stage preserves its own evidence, expands only when every gate passes for the current cohort, stops automatically when telemetry or a critical signal fails, and restores an already-tested compatible artifact.
variants.prompt: The team is assembling the evidence needed before the first canary device is enrolled. Put the pre-release work in order.

items.text: Test clean install, upgrade, interrupted update, corrupt download, low-storage behavior, and rollback.
Soak representative devices long enough to expose throttling, memory growth, and battery impact.
Compare the candidate with the accepted model on global, slice-level, and safety-critical quality gates.
Sign the candidate and bind its hash to metadata, preprocessing, labels, runtime, and compatibility policy.
Enroll hardware canaries that span the support matrix and begin observing cohort gates.

variants.hint: Which artifact identity has to exist before anything can be installed or compared?
variants.explanation: Binding the hash first makes every later result attributable to one exact bundle, which is what lets a canary failure be traced to a specific artifact.

variants.title: Size the device envelope
variants.context: Storage, memory, and latency are separate checks. The guarded memory ceiling is the memory available to the process times one minus the reserve. Update storage demand is the candidate bundle plus the retained known-good bundle. Latency margin is the product deadline minus the measured warm p95.
variants.prompt: A product deadline allows 120 ms end to end. On the target cohort the measured warm p50 is 52 ms and the warm p95 is 86 ms. What is the latency margin?
variants.hint: The gate is written against the tail measurement, not the typical one.
variants.explanation: Latency margin is the product deadline minus the measured warm p95, here 120 minus 86, because the deadline must hold for the tail of real invocations.

mistakes.feedback: That uses the warm p50; the margin is defined against the p95.
That adds the deadline and the measurement instead of subtracting.

variants.title: Size the device envelope
variants.context: Storage, memory, and latency are separate checks. The guarded memory ceiling is the memory available to the process times one minus the reserve. Update storage demand is the candidate bundle plus the retained known-good bundle. Latency margin is the product deadline minus the measured warm p95.
variants.prompt: A process on one cohort has 640 MiB available and the release policy reserves 20 percent as headroom. What is the guarded memory ceiling?
variants.hint: The reserve is carved out of the available memory before anything is compared against it.
variants.explanation: The guarded ceiling is memory available times one minus the reserve, here 640 times 0.8, and the app baseline plus model peak must fit under it.

mistakes.feedback: That is the reserve itself rather than the memory left for the process.
That adds the reserve instead of subtracting it from what is available.

variants.title: Size the device envelope
variants.context: Storage, memory, and latency are separate checks. The guarded memory ceiling is the memory available to the process times one minus the reserve. Update storage demand is the candidate bundle plus the retained known-good bundle. Latency margin is the product deadline minus the measured warm p95.
variants.prompt: A candidate install bundle is 96 MiB and the known-good bundle already on the device is 88 MiB and must stay available for rollback. What is the update storage demand?
variants.hint: A release is only reversible if the fallback is still on the device.
variants.explanation: Update storage demand is the candidate bundle plus the retained known-good bundle, because deleting the fallback to make room removes the offline rollback path.

mistakes.feedback: That counts only the candidate and assumes the known-good bundle can be deleted.
That is the size difference between the bundles, not the space both of them occupy.

variants.title: Declare the failure behavior
variants.context: Failure behavior on a device must be explicit rather than emergent. Each failure has a declared response: reject, fall back, cancel, shed, abstain, or continue locally with bounded telemetry.
variants.prompt: Match each on-device failure to the behavior the design must declare for it.

pairs.label: Model load fails
pairs.detail: Reject the candidate and serve from the local known-good path.

pairs.label: The accelerator rejects an operator
pairs.detail: Refuse to accept an unmeasured CPU fallback as a passing path.

pairs.label: The deadline expires
pairs.detail: Cancel or discard the late work and use the bounded product fallback.

pairs.label: Memory pressure rises
pairs.detail: Shed inference work before the host application becomes unstable.

variants.hint: Ask what the product does for the user in each case, not what the log line says.
variants.explanation: Explicit failure behavior is what keeps a degraded device predictable, because an undeclared fallback is an unmeasured configuration in production.

variants.title: Declare the failure behavior
variants.context: Failure behavior on a device must be explicit rather than emergent. Each failure has a declared response: reject, fall back, cancel, shed, abstain, or continue locally with bounded telemetry.
variants.prompt: Match each runtime or fleet condition to the required response.

pairs.label: The output is invalid or low confidence
pairs.detail: Abstain or route to an approved deterministic behavior.

pairs.label: Connectivity disappears
pairs.detail: Keep serving locally where allowed and bound telemetry retention.

pairs.label: A canary cohort stops reporting
pairs.detail: Stop promotion instead of reading silence as health.

pairs.label: A critical signal crosses its declared limit
pairs.detail: Roll the affected devices back to a tested compatible artifact.

variants.hint: Each condition already has a declared limit; the match is what happens when it is crossed.
variants.explanation: The release controller is a separate authority from the serving path, which is why it can halt and reverse a rollout the device itself still considers healthy.

variants.title: Declare the failure behavior
variants.context: Failure behavior on a device must be explicit rather than emergent. Each failure has a declared response: reject, fall back, cancel, shed, abstain, or continue locally with bounded telemetry.
variants.prompt: Match each lifecycle event to the action it forces before release can continue.

pairs.label: A download arrives corrupt
pairs.detail: Reject the artifact and keep the known-good bundle in place.

pairs.label: Storage is too low to hold both bundles
pairs.detail: Fail the update rather than deleting the rollback target.

pairs.label: The OS ships a driver update
pairs.detail: Re-run compatibility and performance evidence for that cohort.

pairs.label: A signing key is due for rotation
pairs.detail: Rehearse the rotation before an incident rather than during one.

variants.hint: The rule is the same each time: never trade away the recovery path to finish an update.
variants.explanation: Old artifacts are retired only when the fleet no longer needs them for recovery, so an update that would erase the fallback fails instead.

variants.title: Prove the execution path
variants.context: A runtime is chosen after the execution path is proven, not from a feature list. Operator support, accelerator partitioning, package size, per-cohort loading, first-run compilation, and the ability to restore a known-good version are all part of the decision.
variants.prompt: Profiling shows two graph regions of an ONNX Runtime candidate falling back to the CPU on one hardware cohort. What should the team do?
options: Accept it, because a CPU fallback returns identical outputs to the accelerated path.
Treat the partitioned graph as its own configuration and re-profile latency and memory on that cohort.
Drop the cohort from the support matrix so the accelerated path is the only one shipped.
optionFeedback: Identical outputs say nothing about the latency, memory, and energy the fallback consumes.
Correct: execution-provider partitioning changes the measured path, so that cohort needs its own evidence.
Removing a supported cohort to avoid measuring it abandons users rather than resolving the risk.
variants.hint: Ask which graph regions actually run where on this device.
variants.explanation: Unsupported operators push graph regions onto a slower fallback, which changes both latency and memory, so the partitioned path is profiled as its own configuration.

variants.title: Prove the execution path
variants.context: A runtime is chosen after the execution path is proven, not from a feature list. Operator support, accelerator partitioning, package size, per-cohort loading, first-run compilation, and the ability to restore a known-good version are all part of the decision.
variants.prompt: A team wants to build one TensorRT engine on a workstation and ship that same engine to every NVIDIA edge cohort. What is the correct position?
options: Ship the single engine and let each device recompile it if the load fails.
Ship the single engine and rely on the load failure as the rollback trigger.
Build and validate an engine per cohort, since serialized engines are not portable by default.
optionFeedback: Recompilation on the device is not a guaranteed behavior and would land in the user-visible latency budget.
Using load failure as the plan means every device in a mismatched cohort fails before anything is learned.
Correct: TensorRT engines are compiled for specific hardware and are not portable across platforms by default.
variants.hint: Ask whether the artifact you ship is a model or a compiled binary for one target.
variants.explanation: A serialized engine is target-specific and must be treated like executable code, so it is built, validated, and signed per cohort.

variants.title: Prove the execution path
variants.context: A runtime is chosen after the execution path is proven, not from a feature list. Operator support, accelerator partitioning, package size, per-cohort loading, first-run compilation, and the ability to restore a known-good version are all part of the decision.
variants.prompt: A reduced operator build is proposed to shrink the shipped application. What does the release evidence need?
options: Ship it to canaries first and treat any missing operator as a normal runtime error.
Verify every operator the candidate uses is present and measure the final application package.
Quote the model artifact size, since the runtime delta is the same on every device.
optionFeedback: A missing operator surfaces as a load failure on real user devices, which is exactly what pre-release verification prevents.
Correct: a reduced build is only safe if the operator set covers the model, and size is judged on the package.
Artifact size is a storage input and says nothing about the runtime added to the binary.
variants.hint: The user installs the application, not the model file.
variants.explanation: Packaging is measured on the final application rather than the model artifact, and a reduced runtime build must be checked against the candidate's operator set.
